title: Pai Gow Poker in Canada: Rules, Odds and Strategy
excerpt: Pai Gow Poker is the slowest, push-heaviest game on the casino floor. Here are the rules, the house edge and the setting strategy Canadian players need in 2026.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
If you want your bankroll to last, Pai Gow Poker is arguably the best game in any Canadian online casino lobby. It is slow, it pushes constantly, and the house edge sits in respectable company alongside blackjack and baccarat. It is also the least understood game on the floor, which is precisely why so few players give it a chance. Pai Gow Poker rewards patience over excitement, and once you understand how the hand-setting decision works, it becomes one of the most relaxing ways to spend a bankroll online.

This guide covers how the game works, what it costs you in house edge, and the setting rules that turn a coin-flip into a genuinely competitive bet.

How Pai Gow Poker works

The game uses a standard 52-card deck plus one joker. You are dealt seven cards, and your job is to split them into two poker hands: a five-card hand, traditionally called the high or back hand, and a two-card hand, called the low or front hand.

There is one absolute rule governing the split. The five-card hand must rank higher than the two-card hand. Set them the other way around and the hand is fouled, which means an automatic loss. Online the software will usually refuse to let you commit an illegal setting, but it is worth understanding why the rule exists: it is the constraint that makes the decision interesting.

The dealer sets their own seven cards according to a fixed published rule known as the house way. Then the hands are compared:

  • Win both comparisons and you win the bet, less a commission on most versions.
  • Lose both comparisons and you lose the bet.
  • Split, winning one and losing one, and the hand pushes. Your stake comes back untouched.
  • Exact ties in a comparison go to the dealer, which is where a meaningful chunk of the house edge lives.

That push outcome is the defining feature. A very large share of Pai Gow hands end in a push, which is why a session can run a long time on a modest bankroll. If you are used to the swings of slots, the experience is almost eerily calm. Players coming from other table games will find the rhythm closer to what we describe in our online poker games guide, though the strategy has nothing in common with real poker.

The joker and how it behaves

The joker is not fully wild. It functions as an ace, except that it may also be used to complete a straight, a flush or a straight flush. That restriction matters: a joker plus a pair does not give you three of a kind, it gives you a pair plus an ace. New players routinely misread their own hand because of this.

House edge and commission

Played with correct strategy, Pai Gow Poker's house edge lands in the low single digits, comparable to the better bets in online blackjack and clearly better than roulette on an American wheel. Two factors drive it.

The first is the commission, traditionally five percent on winning hands. Because so many hands push and the commission applies only to wins, its real cost is smaller than it looks, but it is the single biggest contributor to the edge. Some online variants replace the commission with a rule tweak instead, such as paying even money but losing a specific hand type. Those variants are not automatically better or worse; check the rules screen before you assume.

The second is copy hands. When your hand exactly ties the dealer's, the dealer wins. Ties are far more common in the two-card front hand than intuition suggests, and this quietly tilts a meaningful number of otherwise-push hands into losses.

The banking option

In some live-dealer Pai Gow implementations you are offered the chance to bank the hand, taking the dealer's side of the copy-hand rule. Banking flips a real edge in your favour, which is why it is offered only intermittently and often requires sufficient funds to cover other bets at the table. Where it is available and affordable, taking your turn to bank is the single most valuable decision in the game. In most online RNG versions it is not offered at all.

Setting strategy: the rules that matter

Optimal Pai Gow strategy is genuinely complex, with published charts running to dozens of branches. But the vast majority of the available edge comes from a handful of principles, and a player who follows these will give up only a fraction of a percent to a perfect strategist.

The governing idea is balance. Your goal is not to maximise either hand. It is to maximise the probability of winning both comparisons, which usually means making the two-card hand as strong as legally possible without gutting the five-card hand.

The core rules:

  • No pair, nothing playable. Put your highest card in the back hand and your next two highest in the front. This is the most common hand you will be dealt.
  • One pair. Keep the pair in the back and play your two highest remaining cards in front. Almost never split a single pair.
  • Two pair. This is the decision that separates competent players from poor ones. As a general rule, split them, putting the higher pair in the back and the lower pair in front, unless the pairs are both very small and you hold a strong ace to play in front. Keeping two small pairs together in the back with a weak front hand loses far more often than it wins.
  • Three pair. Always play the highest pair in front and the other two pairs in the back.
  • Three of a kind. Keep it in the back, except with three aces, where you split off an ace to make a powerful front hand.
  • Straights, flushes and full houses. Play the made hand in the back only if you cannot break it while keeping the back hand strong. With a full house, always split it: the three of a kind wins the back, the pair wins the front.

If you take nothing else from a strategy chart, take the full house rule and the two-pair rule. Between them they account for most of the money recreational players give away.

Fortune and side bets

Nearly every online Pai Gow table offers a bonus side bet paying on rare seven-card combinations. The payouts look attractive and the house edge on these wagers is dramatically worse than the base game, typically several times higher. They are entertainment, not strategy. If you enjoy them, treat the stake as an expense rather than a bet, and keep it small relative to your main wager.

Who Pai Gow is for

Pai Gow Poker suits a specific type of player: someone who wants a long session, low variance, a decision to make on every hand, and a house edge they can respect. It is a poor fit for anyone chasing a big score, because the push rate that protects your bankroll also caps your upside.
